title: The Mystery of the Voynich Manuscript
summary: The Voynich manuscript, Beinecke MS 408 at Yale, is a small book of some 240 pages of calfskin, drawn on almost every page, in a script found in no other book. In 2009 the University of Arizona dated four slivers of its...

places.name: Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library, Yale University, New Haven
places.note: Where the manuscript is kept as Beinecke MS 408, since H. P. Kraus gave it to Yale in 1969; it has left the building only once (Beinecke).

places.name: Prague
places.note: Where Georg Baresch wrote to Athanasius Kircher about the book in 1639 and Johannes Marcus Marci sent it to him in 1665 (letters, tr. Philip Neal); Rudolf the Second's court, where Jacobus de Tepenec, who signed the book, was the emperor's pharmacist. A point in the city, not a building.

places.name: Collegio Romano, Rome
places.note: Kircher's Jesuit college in Rome, where Marci's letter of 1665 and the book were sent. Afterwards the book was in Jesuit libraries until Wilfrid Voynich bought it from the Jesuits near Rome in 1912 (the exact place is disputed).

places.name: Augsburg
places.note: Where a doctor sold Rudolf the Second some manuscripts in 1599 for a price recorded as 600 gold florins, and where a small barrel of strange books was held up in 1600 (Stefan Guzy, via The Art Newspaper 2023; Zandbergen). That our book was among them is Guzy's suggestion and cannot be proved.

places.name: University of Arizona, Tucson
places.note: The radiocarbon laboratory where Greg Hodgins's four samples were dated, 1404 to 1438 (University of Arizona, 2011). The samples were cut at Yale in 2009.

places.name: Soho Square, London
places.note: Wilfrid Voynich's rare book shop, photographed about 1899; he had reached London in 1890 (Zandbergen). The year stands for the photograph.

title: How Chess Began, and Why the Queen Got Her Power
summary: For about nine hundred years, the piece we call the queen moved one square at a time; in Persian and Arabic chess it was the king's counsellor. The oldest clear Indian words about the game are a royal pun of the early 600s on...

places.name: Afrasiab (old Samarkand), Uzbekistan
places.note: Where Yuri Buryakov found, in 1977, the seven little ivory figures that Jean-Louis Cazaux calls the earliest known chess pieces; a coin in the same layer points to about the year 700. The marker is the site, not the trench.

places.name: Baghdad, Iraq
places.note: The court of the caliphs, where chess players first have names and records (the 800s and 900s): al-Suli, who died in 946, and the caliph al-Radi.

places.name: Constantinople (Istanbul)
places.note: The emperor Nicephorus wrote from here to Harun al-Rashid, about 803, in a letter that used chess for an insult (al-Tabari).

places.name: Aachen, Germany
places.note: Charlemagne's palace: the elephant Abul Abaz arrived here in July 802 (the Frankish royal annals).

places.name: Einsiedeln, Switzerland
places.note: A Latin poem on chess copied at the monastery around the year 1000 calls the counsellor regina, the queen.

places.name: La Seu d'Urgell, Catalonia
places.note: Count Ermengol of Urgell, whose will dated 1008 leaves his chessmen to the monastery of Saint Giles.

places.name: Florence, Italy
places.note: Peter Damian's letter of about 1061 tells of the bishop of Florence who spent an evening at chess.

places.name: Westminster, London
places.note: The royal Exchequer, whose name, an official explained around 1180, came from its shape, similar to that of a chess board.

places.name: Valencia, Spain
places.note: Scachs d'amor, the earliest known game with the new moves, a poem by three Valencian poets, dated by Ricardo Calvo to between 1470 and 1490 (the year on the map is the start of that range).

places.name: Salamanca, Spain
places.note: Luis de Lucena's book, around 1497: the oldest printed book on playing chess that survives.

title: Who Were the Sea Peoples?
summary: The Sea Peoples is the name French scholars of the nineteenth century gave to the peoples an Egyptian pharaoh said had come from islands, from across the sea, as the Bronze Age was ending. Merneptah's inscription at Karnak names...

places.name: Ugarit (Ras Shamra), Syria
places.note: A trading port on the Syrian coast, a vassal of the Hittite king. Its clay letters ask for grain and report seven enemy ships (Georgiou 1979, Cline 2015); the city was destroyed and arrowheads were found in its walls amid burned houses (Cline 2015). The year is only a marker for the last years of the city: the letters are not dated to a year.

places.name: Medinet Habu, temple of Ramesses III, near Luxor, Egypt
places.note: Ramesses III had the war of his eighth year carved on his temple here: the inscription of year eight and the sea battle on the north wall (Edgerton and Wilson 1936). 1177 B.C. is Eric Cline's dating.

places.name: Karnak, Thebes, Egypt
places.note: Merneptah's Great Karnak Inscription names Ekwesh, Teresh, Luka, Sherden and Shekelesh, "Northerners coming from all lands" (Breasted 1906). 1207 B.C. is Eric Cline's dating.

places.name: Hattusa (Boğazkale), Turkey
places.note: The Hittite capital, burned early in the twelfth century B.C. (excavations led by Jürgen Seeher); Trevor Bryce writes that it was probably little more than a ghost town by then and suggests the final blow may have come from the Kaska, from the north. The year is a marker for "early in the twelfth century".

places.name: Gordion, Turkey
places.note: About 230 km west of Hattusa. Its juniper timbers show the only run of back to back extreme dry years between about 1270 and 1135 B.C.: three in a row, about 1198 to 1196 B.C., give or take three years (Manning et al., Nature 2023).

places.name: Ashkelon, Israel
places.note: The team digging here announced the first Philistine cemetery ever found in 2016; more than 210 people have been excavated. DNA from ten of 108 samples (Feldman et al. 2019) shows a European-related ancestry in four infants buried under early Iron Age houses (not in the cemetery).

places.name: Hazor, Israel
places.note: The palace and the temples were burned; the rest of the city was essentially untouched. Who did that is not known (Cline 2015).

places.name: Dor, Israel
places.note: Called a city of the Tjeker (Breasted: Thekel) in the Report of Wenamun, whose king sent the envoy bread, wine and beef (Breasted 1906).

title: The Mystery of Rome's Lost Legion
summary: Around A.D. 108 the Ninth Legion, Hispana, put its name on a great stone at York. It is the last dated trace of the legion anywhere in Britain; in 122 the Sixth Legion arrived from the Rhine, and no ancient writer we have tells...
tags: What Happened to the Ninth Legion

places.name: York (Eboracum), England
places.note: The Ninth's fortress, built A.D. 71 to 74 (City of York HER). The slab RIB 665, dated A.D. 107/108 by Trajan's titles, came up in 1854 from seven metres below King's Square; the last dated record of the Ninth in Britain.

places.name: Nijmegen, Netherlands
places.note: Tiles of the Ninth from the Roman fortress, published since the 1960s; a bronze inscribed LEG HISP IX from Ewijk nearby, dated about A.D. 125, is in Museum Het Valkhof.

places.name: Vindolanda, near Hadrian's Wall, England
places.note: The tombstone of Titus Annius, centurion of the First Cohort of Tungrians, "killed in war" (RIB 3364), was found here in 1997. The stone does not say which war.

places.name: Silchester (Calleva Atrebatum), England
places.note: The Reverend J. G. Joyce found the wingless bronze eagle here in 1866; it inspired The Eagle of the Ninth. George Boon (1957) thought it more likely came from a statue of Jupiter or of an emperor.

places.name: Newcastle upon Tyne, the Swing Bridge, England
places.note: The Sixth Legion's altars to Neptune and to Ocean (RIB 1319 and 1320) from the bridge over the Tyne were found in the river at the Swing Bridge in 1875 and 1903.

places.name: Elegeia, Armenia (site uncertain)
places.note: Where, Dio says, a Parthian king destroyed a Roman legion, "the whole force, leaders and all", about thirty years after the war in Judaea. The site is not securely located: the point is only a marker on the Erzurum plain.

title: Tanzwut: The Dancing Plague of 1518
summary: In July 1518 a woman in Strasbourg began to dance; within four weeks, a family chronicle of the time says, more than four hundred people were dancing. The physicians called it a natural sickness. The city gave the dancers guild...

places.name: Strasbourg, France
places.note: Where the dancing began in July 1518. A family chronicle of the time places the first dancers by the council's stable and in the guild halls of the tanners and the carpenters, and, in Specklin's later account, stages on the horse market and the grain market (their exact sites are not marked here). The marker is the cathedral.

places.name: Saint Vitus cave (the Hollow Stone), above Saverne
places.note: Saint Vitus' shrine in a cave in the hills behind Saverne, where the council sent the dancers on wagons; Specklin says they were given little crosses and red shoes there. The marker is the town of Saverne, not the cave itself.

places.name: Rottweil, Germany
places.note: Its town law of 1485 fined anyone who cursed another with the fever or Saint Vitus' dance three shillings (Martin 1914, p. 121).

places.name: Augsburg, Germany
places.note: Home of the merchant Wilhelm Rem, whose chronicle of the time says that about fifteen people were seized by the dance in a day in Strasbourg.

title: The Mystery of Stonehenge's Altar Stone
summary: The Altar Stone lies at the heart of Stonehenge: a six tonne slab of pale green sandstone, broken and pinned under two fallen stones of the Great Trilithon, that nobody is allowed to sample. In 2024 tiny mineral grains in chips...
tags: Where Did the Altar Stone Come From

places.name: Stonehenge
places.note: Where the Altar Stone lies, near the centre, under two fallen stones of the Great Trilithon. When it arrived is uncertain: possibly during the second construction phase, around 2620 to 2480 B.C. (Clarke et al., Nature 2024); the year is approximate.

places.name: West Woods, near Marlborough
places.note: Where most of the giant sarsens came from, about 25 km north of Stonehenge (Nash et al. 2020, as cited by Clarke et al. 2024 and Clarke, Veness et al. 2026). The year stands for that study. Coordinates approximate.

places.name: Craig Rhos-y-felin, Preseli Hills
places.note: One of the two bluestone quarries in west Wales, about 225 km from Stonehenge, with stone wedges still in the cracks (Parker Pearson et al. 2024). The year is approximate: quarrying "centuries before and around 3000 bc" (same paper). Coordinates approximate.

places.name: Carn Goedog, Preseli Hills
places.note: The other bluestone quarry in west Wales (Parker Pearson et al. 2024). The year is approximate, as for Craig Rhos-y-felin. Coordinates approximate.

places.name: Stones of Stenness, Orkney
places.note: One of Orkney's own stone circles, tested as the Altar Stone's source in 2024: no match (Bevins et al. 2024, via Aberystwyth University, 5 September 2024). The year stands for the test. Coordinates approximate.

places.name: Ring of Brodgar, Orkney
places.note: Tested with the Stones of Stenness in 2024: no match (Bevins et al. 2024). The year stands for the test. Coordinates approximate.

places.name: Caithness
places.note: The county on the Scottish mainland whose sandstones gave the closest zircon match in Clarke, Veness et al. 2026 (J. Quaternary Science). No site is pinned: the exact source is, in Pirrie et al. 2026's words, as yet unknown. A point in the county area, not a find spot.

places.name: North Ferriby, on the Humber
places.note: Where the oldest known boats in Britain were found, about 15 m long; the earliest dates from between about 2030 and 1780 B.C. (Parker Pearson et al. 2024). No boat is known from the Altar Stone's age. Coordinates approximate.

places.name: Durrington Walls
places.note: The settlement near Stonehenge whose houses have floor plans unusually like those at Skara Brae (Parker Pearson et al. 2024). The year stands for that comparison; the houses' own dates are not in our sources. Coordinates approximate.

places.name: Skara Brae, Orkney
places.note: Neolithic houses by the Bay of Skaill, compared with Durrington Walls by Parker Pearson et al. 2024. The year stands for that comparison. Coordinates approximate.

title: The Lost Diary of the Great Pyramid
summary: In 2013, between the stones that sealed the boat galleries of a harbour of King Khufu at Wadi al-Jarf, on Egypt's Red Sea coast, Pierre Tallet's team found the oldest inscribed papyri ever discovered in Egypt. Among them is the...
tags: How Was the Great Pyramid Built

places.name: Wadi al-Jarf
places.note: A harbour of King Khufu on the Red Sea coast (Gulf of Suez), with thirty galleries for boats; the papyri were found here in 2013 between the blocking stones of two galleries (Tallet and Marouard 2014). The year stands for the papyri, year 26 or 27 of Khufu, and is approximate. Coordinates approximate.

places.name: Giza: the Great Pyramid (Akhet-Khufu)
places.note: Akhet-Khufu, the Horizon of Khufu: the Great Pyramid and its buildings, where Merer's boats delivered the stone. The year is approximate (late in Khufu's reign).

places.name: Tura quarries
places.note: The white limestone quarries across the Nile, about 17 km from the pyramid (Sheisha et al. 2022), where Merer's section hauled stone at Tura North and Tura South, whose exact positions are not known. Today a military zone. Year approximate; coordinates approximate.

places.name: Heliopolis
places.note: Where Idjeru, director of six, sailed “to bring us food”, coming back three days later with forty sacks of bread (Papyrus B). Year approximate; coordinates approximate (modern Matariya).

places.name: Wadi Maghara, Sinai
places.note: The copper and turquoise mining region of Sinai, reached by Khufu's ships from Wadi al-Jarf (D1.5). The year stands for Khufu's reign and is approximate. Coordinates approximate.

places.name: Hatnub alabaster quarry
places.note: Where the Hatnub mission (Gourdon and Enmarch) announced in 2018 a ramp at 20 percent or more between two staircases with post holes, dated by tool marks and two inscriptions of Khufu at least to his reign. The year stands for the announcement. Coordinates approximate.

title: Easter Island's Heads Have Bodies
summary: Easter Island's famous heads have bodies: from 2010 the Easter Island Statue Project dug two of them down to their bases at the quarry of Rano Raraku, one about seven metres tall and one over eight. Who carved the moai is no...

places.name: Rano Raraku
places.note: The volcano where ninety-five in every hundred statues were cut and about half never left its slopes; the Easter Island Statue Project dug two statues to their bases here from 2010. Coordinates approximate.

places.name: Ahu Te Pito Kura (Paro)
places.note: Where Paro lies, the biggest statue ever set up, almost 10 m and about 74 tonnes, moved about 6 km from the quarry (NOVA after Van Tilburg). When it was set up and when it fell is not in our sources; the year stands for the first European visit. Coordinates approximate.

places.name: Orongo
places.note: The ceremonial centre on Rano Kao from which the crew of HMS Topaze took Hoa Hakananai'a in 1868 (British Museum). Coordinates approximate.

places.name: British Museum, London
places.note: Where Hoa Hakananai'a, one of only fourteen basalt moai, has been since 1869 (British Museum Oc1869,1005.1).

title: The Mystery of the Antikythera Mechanism
summary: Shortly before Easter 1900, sponge divers found a great ship off the Greek island of Antikythera. Among its finds was a box of bronze gears that showed the Sun, the Moon, coming eclipses and the years of the Olympic Games. Under...

places.name: Antikythera
places.note: The small Greek island between Crete and the Peloponnese off which sponge divers found the wreck in 1900, at about 42 metres (Price 1974). The year stands for the wreck, around 60 B.C., give or take ten years. The dot marks the island, not the wreck: we have not read a position for it.

places.name: National Archaeological Museum, Athens
places.note: Where the pieces lay among bronze scraps, and where, in the spring of 1902, a visitor noticed toothed gears and an inscription in mirror writing (IAM 2). The fragments are there today.

places.name: Symi
places.note: Home island of the sponge divers who found the wreck while sailing home from the coast of North Africa (Price 1974). Coordinates approximate.

places.name: Rhodes
places.note: The star calendar on the front fits the latitude of Rhodes or southern Greece (IAM 3); Rhodes had the Halieia games, very probably named on the games dial, and Posidonius. Where the machine was made is not known. The year stands for the machine, second or first century B.C.

places.name: Corinth
places.note: The month names on the back belong to the calendar of Corinth; the research team's later edition leans to Corinth itself or to Epirus (IAM 4). The year stands for the machine and is approximate.

places.name: Dodona
places.note: Sanctuary in Epirus, northwest Greece, whose games, the Naa, are named on the four-year games dial (IAM 4). The year stands for the machine and is approximate.

places.name: Syracuse
places.note: Where Archimedes lived, whose sphere Marcellus's grandfather carried off when Rome took the city (Cicero, De re publica 1.21). In 2008 the research team first pointed to Corinth's colonies in northwest Greece, or to Syracuse, for the calendar; the year stands for that proposal.

title: Warship Rams Found Where Rome Won the First Punic War
summary: Warship rams found where Rome won the First Punic War. Off the Egadi Islands, west of Sicily, in 241 B.C., Rome's last fleet, which Polybius says was paid for by its leading citizens on a promise of repayment if all went well...

places.name: Battle site off Levanzo, Egadi Islands
places.note: Where the rams were found, 70 to 90 metres down, west of Levanzo; the survey area was about 270 square kilometres. The point is placed from one ram's published position (Egadi 6, about 7 km west of Levanzo), not from a survey map.

places.name: Levanzo
places.note: One of the Egadi Islands; the finds lie off its west side.

places.name: Favignana
places.note: The largest of the Egadi Islands. Polybius says Catulus sailed to Aegusa, off Lilybaeum, before the battle; we have no source in hand that identifies Aegusa with a modern island.

places.name: Lilybaeum (Marsala)
places.note: The Carthaginian harbour Rome blockaded, where Hannibal the Rhodian ran the blockade in full view, a few years before the battle.

places.name: Drepana (Trapani)
places.note: Where Carthage captured ninety-three Roman ships in 249 B.C., Polybius says; some scholars think those ships fought again for Carthage in 241. One late writer says Catulus was wounded in the thigh at Drepana.

places.name: Mount Eryx (Erice)
places.note: The mountain where Hamilcar Barca's army was; Hanno's fleet was bringing it grain and supplies.

places.name: Pantelleria
places.note: Ballast stones in the jars found at the battle site came from Pantelleria and North Africa, which points to Carthage.

places.name: Carthage
places.note: Rome's enemy in the First Punic War; it sent Hanno's fleet and then asked for peace.

places.name: Capitoline Museums, Rome (the Fasti)
places.note: The list of triumphs, carved in stone under Augustus, shows a naval triumph for Catulus on 4 October and for Falto two days later.

title: Battle of Adwa: The Treaty Line That Meant Two Things
summary: Battle of Adwa: the treaty line that meant two things. In 1889 Menelik II of Ethiopia and Italy signed the Treaty of Wuchale. In its Italian text, Article 17 says the emperor consents to use Italy's government for all his...

places.name: Adwa
places.note: The town in northern Ethiopia near which the battle was fought on 1 March 1896 (OpenStreetMap coordinates of the town). The battle positions are not placed here: our sources do not let us map them.

places.name: Massawa
places.note: The Red Sea port Italy held when the treaty was signed (OpenStreetMap).

places.name: Amba Alage
places.note: Where, that winter, the Italian commander died with 1,500 of his African soldiers and 20 Italians (Davis). The point is the nearby town; the mountain is a few kilometres away.

places.name: Mekele
places.note: An Italian garrison here surrendered when its water ran out (Davis).

places.name: Addis Ababa
places.note: Where the peace was signed on 26 October 1896: the Treaty of Wuchale annulled, Ethiopia recognised as a sovereign and independent state.

title: The King of Aksum Who Changed Gods on His Coins
summary: The king of Aksum who changed gods on his coins. Ezana ruled Aksum, on the northern edge of the Ethiopian plateau, in the fourth century A.D. His early gold carries the crescent and disc of the old religion, and on his stones he...

places.name: Aksum
places.note: Ezana's royal city on the northern edge of the Ethiopian plateau, today a town in Tigray, Ethiopia (coordinates of the modern town). The year stands for Ezana's reign, about 330 to 360 A.D.

places.name: Adulis
places.note: The Red Sea port described in the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, first century A.D., eight days from the city of the Auxumites (the archaeological site near Zula, Eritrea). The year is approximate.

places.name: Tyre
places.note: Home of the philosopher Meropius and the two boys Frumentius and Aedesius in Rufinus' story. Rufinus gives no year; the year stands for Ezana's reign.

places.name: Alexandria
places.note: Where Bishop Athanasius made Frumentius bishop; around 356 Athanasius quoted the emperor's letter to Ezana and Sazana.

title: 10 Famous Battles, Ranked by What They Changed
summary: Ten famous battles, from Kadesh, about 1274 B.C., to Adwa in 1896, ranked by one thing: what was different afterwards, and for how long. Cannae comes last: Rome lost the battle and won the war. Hastings comes first: a new king...

places.name: Hastings: Battle Abbey, on the traditional site
places.note: Number one. By tradition the English stood on the hill where the abbey was later built; nothing from the battle has been found at the abbey (English Heritage)

places.name: Gaugamela, northern Iraq (field not found)
places.note: Number two. The point marks only the region: the field has not been found

places.name: Horns of Hattin, above the Sea of Galilee
places.note: Number three. The battle of 4 July 1187; weapons have been found along the march route

places.name: Kalkriese, Germany
places.note: Number four, the Teutoburg Forest. A Roman army did die at Kalkriese; whether it is the battle of A.D. 9 is disputed

places.name: Adwa, Ethiopia
places.note: Number five. The battle of 1 March 1896, in the hills near the town

places.name: Ain Jalut (Ma'ayan Harod), at the foot of Mount Gilboa
places.note: Number six. The spring in the Jezreel valley; the battle of 3 September 1260

places.name: The strait of Salamis, Greece
places.note: Number seven. The sea battle of 480 B.C.

places.name: Takashima, Imari Bay (Hakata Bay battles)
places.note: Number eight. Divers have confirmed three wrecks of the 1281 invasion fleet off the island; the first invasion came to Hakata Bay in 1274

places.name: Kadesh on the Orontes (Tell Nebi Mend), Syria
places.note: Number nine. The year B.C. depends on the chronology, so about 1274 B.C.

places.name: Cannae, the hill of Canne by the Ofanto
places.note: Number ten. The traditional site; where exactly the battle was fought is still argued

title: Salamis, 480 BC: Xerxes' Scribes Took Names
summary: The Battle of Salamis, 480 B.C., in three records that do not agree: Herodotus, who tells how Xerxes watched from below Mount Aegaleos while his scribes wrote down the names of captains who did well; Aeschylus' play Persians...

places.name: The strait of Salamis
places.note: Where the fleets fought, probably late September 480 B.C. The exact lines of the fleets are disputed; today's coastline differs somewhat from the ancient shore.

places.name: Mount Aegaleos
places.note: Herodotus says Xerxes sat beneath the mountain opposite Salamis called Aegaleos, and his scribes wrote down the names of captains who did well. Aeschylus puts him on a high headland by the sea. The exact spot is not known.

places.name: Psyttaleia
places.note: The islet at the mouth of the strait where, Herodotus says, many of the Persians landed during the night before the battle.

places.name: The Acropolis, Athens
places.note: Where Herodotus says the Athenians fed a sacred snake a honey cake every month. The Persians took the Acropolis and burned it.

places.name: Laurion
places.note: The silver mines whose windfall, ten drachmas a man, Themistocles talked the Athenians into spending on two hundred ships.

places.name: Delphi
places.note: The oracle that answered: divine Salamis, you will bring death to women's sons. The Greek victory monument stood here; its bronze column is now in Istanbul.

places.name: Troezen
places.note: Where the stone with the decree was found. The decree sends the women and children to Troezen. The stone was carved about two hundred years after Salamis.

places.name: The Serpent Column, Hippodrome, Istanbul
places.note: The bronze column of the Greek victory monument from Delphi. Herodotus says the Tenians were engraved on it for the ship that deserted and told the Greeks they were surrounded.

places.name: Halicarnassus (Bodrum)
places.note: Artemisia's city, and the city Herodotus came from.

places.name: Tenos (Tinos)
places.note: The island of the ship that deserted the Persian side before the battle.

title: Ramesses II Said He Won the Battle of Kadesh Alone
summary: The Battle of Kadesh, about 1274 B.C., from Ramesses II's own poem, official record and relief captions, and from the Hittite side: the two Bedouin who lied, the beaten scouts, the ambush on the division of Re, the poem's lone...

places.name: Kadesh on the Orontes (Tell Nebi Mend), Syria
places.note: The city of the battle, about 1274 B.C.; today the mound of Tell Nebi Mend. Ramesses camped on its northwest side with the division of Amun; the Hittite army stood drawn up behind the city. Kadesh was not taken. Where exactly the camp and the fighting were is not known.

places.name: Aleppo
places.note: Where the two Bedouin said the Hittite king was, far to the north; Ramesses' own record says they said it falsely.

places.name: Damascus
places.note: Trevor Bryce writes that after the battle the Egyptians were forced to retreat south, with the Hittite army in pursuit, as far as the region of Damascus.

places.name: Hattusa, the Hittite capital (Bogazkale, Turkey)
places.note: The Hittite archive where clay versions of the treaty and Ramesses' letter about Kadesh were found.

places.name: Abu Simbel, the great temple of Ramesses II
places.note: The Kadesh relief on the north wall of the great hall: the camp, the council, the beaten scouts. Its caption gives the Hittite reserve as 9,000.

places.name: The Ramesseum, Thebes
places.note: Ramesses' temple at Thebes. Its caption gives the Hittite reserve as 8,000; Egypt carved its copy of the treaty here and at Karnak.

places.name: Luxor temple, Thebes
places.note: Kadesh reliefs on the first pylon; among the troops coming up, a fragment of text reads: Arrival of the vizier.

places.name: Karnak, Thebes
places.note: The Egyptian copy of the treaty of Ramesses' twenty-first year is carved on a wall here.

places.name: Abydos, temple of Ramesses II
places.note: One of the temples where Breasted (1906) records Kadesh texts or reliefs.

title: How Weapons Evolved: From Sling to Cannon
summary: How weapons evolved from the sling to the cannon, told from the earliest evidence that survives (a find, a text or a picture), not from dates of invention: the bows of Holmegaard and the Iceman, Tutankhamun's slings, the catapult...

places.name: Sibudu Cave
places.note: Small stone points that Marlize Lombard and Laurel Phillipson argue tipped arrows, about 64,000 years ago (Antiquity 84, 2010); the year shown is that figure converted, and it is argued, not certain.

places.name: Holmegaard bog
places.note: Remains of five elm bows from about 7000 B.C., some of Europe's oldest bows (National Museum of Denmark).

places.name: Tisenjoch, Ötztal Alps
places.note: The Iceman died here over 5,300 years ago with an unfinished yew bow and fourteen arrows, two of them finished (South Tyrol Museum of Archaeology); the year shown is that figure converted.

places.name: Perugia
places.note: Lead sling bullets from the siege of 41 to 40 B.C., one inscribed "You're starving, and you're hiding it from me" (Zangemeister 1885; our sling-bullet episode).

places.name: Syracuse
places.note: Where, Diodorus writes, Dionysius gathered craftsmen and the catapult was invented; 399 B.C. is the standard conversion of Diodorus's year.

places.name: Motya
places.note: Bolt-shooters fired from the shore at the siege, archers and slingers on the ships (Diodorus 14.50.4); the siege is conventionally dated 397 or 396 B.C.

places.name: Terracotta Army, near Xi'an
places.note: 216 bronze crossbow triggers from Pit 1, made in batches (Li et al., Antiquity 88, 2014). Year shown: the end of the Warring States period (476 to 221 B.C.), when trigger crossbows came in; the pit's own date is not discussed in this episode.

places.name: Thessaloniki
places.note: Bishop John described the Avars' machines with slings; the siege is dated 586 or 597, scholars disagree.

places.name: Stirling Castle
places.note: Edward I's Warwolf, almost certainly a trebuchet, and the oriel he paid for so the queen and her ladies could watch the assault (Bain, Calendar of Documents relating to Scotland).

places.name: Xanadu (Shangdu)
places.note: A small bronze gun found here carries a date matching 1298 and a serial number; perhaps the oldest surviving gun whose date is beyond doubt (Andrade).

places.name: Florence
places.note: On 11 February 1326 the city ordered iron balls and cannons of metal (Tiberini 2022).

places.name: Rouen
places.note: A French letter of July 1338 records an iron pot gun sent from Rouen with 48 arrows, a pound of saltpetre and half a pound of sulphur (Morton 2014).

places.name: Tenochtitlan (Mexico City)
places.note: Cortés, short of ammunition, had a trebuchet built; its first stone went straight up, came back down and smashed it (Chevedden et al. 1995).

places.name: The Solent, off Portsmouth
places.note: The Mary Rose sank here in 1545 with 91 guns and 250 longbows on her lists (Mary Rose Trust); position approximate.

title: Domesday Book: Why Was It Made?
summary: Domesday Book, the survey William the Conqueror ordered at Gloucester at Christmas 1085: the Danish threat of that winter, how the survey worked, the questions of the Ely inquest, one entry decoded (Cogges and Wadard), Exon...

places.name: Gloucester
places.note: King William held court here for five days at Christmas 1085 and ordered the survey (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle; The National Archives).

places.name: Salisbury (the Chronicle's Sarum)
places.note: On 1 August 1086 the landholders of any account bowed to William here and swore him oaths (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle). For James Holt, the climax of the survey. The marker is approximate.

places.name: Hereford
places.note: Robert, Bishop of Hereford, wrote at the time of the second team sent to find fault with the first survey.

places.name: Ely
places.note: The questions of the survey survive at the head of the collection known as the Ely inquest.

places.name: Cogges, Oxfordshire
places.note: Held from Bishop Odo of Bayeux by Wadard: five hides, land for eight ploughs, a mill worth ten shillings, worth ten pounds then and now.

places.name: Exeter
places.note: Exeter Cathedral keeps Exon Domesday, the earliest surviving manuscript of the survey (Stephen Baxter).

places.name: Winchester
places.note: The book was first kept in the treasury here and first called the Book of Winchester; the city itself is not in Great Domesday (The National Archives).

places.name: Kew (The National Archives)
places.note: Where Great and Little Domesday are kept today.

title: Teutoburg Forest, AD 9: What Kalkriese Found
summary: The Battle of the Teutoburg Forest, A.D. 9, and the field at Kalkriese: a Roman mule still wearing its bell under a collapsed bank; what Velleius, Tacitus, Dio, Florus and Suetonius say, none of whom was there; Varus, Arminius...

places.name: Kalkriese, the Oberesch field
places.note: Where the passage between Kalkriese hill and the Great Bog is narrowest. A Roman army was destroyed here around the time of Varus; whether it was his, or Caecina's six years later, is disputed.

places.name: The hills called the Teutoburg Forest today
places.note: Tacitus names the Teutoburg forest but never says exactly where it was. These hills, says the Kalkriese museum, were only renamed after it in the seventeenth century. The pin marks the region.

places.name: Osnabrück
places.note: Tony Clunn asked the county archaeologist of Osnabrück, Wolfgang Schlüter, for permission to search with a metal detector in March 1987.

places.name: Near Xanten, on the Rhine
places.note: The gravestone of Marcus Caelius, centurion of the Eighteenth Legion, who fell in the Varian War, was found near here in 1620.

places.name: Dangstetten
places.note: The old base of the Nineteenth Legion. In 2026 a metal study found the Kalkriese bronzes close to those from here.

places.name: Rennes, France
places.note: A coin in the museum here has the VAR stamp struck over a mark of the emperor Tiberius, as reported.

title: Hattin, 1187: The Battle That Lost the True Cross
summary: The Battle of Hattin, 4 July 1187, from the sources on both sides: Saladin's words to his son, "until that tent falls"; Reynald of Chatillon's attack on a caravan during a truce; Tiberias stormed to draw the Franks out; the...

places.name: Horns of Hattin, above the Sea of Galilee
places.note: The double summit near the village of Hattin where the kingdom of Jerusalem lost its army, its king and the True Cross on 4 July 1187. The last knights held 'a hill near Hattin' around the king's tent (Ibn al-Athir); exactly where the lines stood is not known. Saladin's Dome of Victory stood on the southern summit.

places.name: Springs of Sepphoris (Zippori)
places.note: The Frankish camp before the march; in 2021 archaeologists reported a crusader camp at the springs, where Frankish armies gathered more than once. The army left on Friday, 3 July 1187.

places.name: Tiberias, on the Sea of Galilee
places.note: Stormed by Saladin on 2 July 1187; only the citadel held out, with the wife of Raymond of Tripoli and her children inside.

places.name: Turan
places.note: The village near the one small spring the army passed on 3 July; measured in 1989 for Benjamin Kedar at 180 litres an hour.

places.name: Kerak castle, beyond the Dead Sea
places.note: Castle of Reynald of Chatillon, who attacked a caravan coming from Egypt during a truce, probably early in 1187. Where the caravan was attacked is not known.

places.name: Tyre
places.note: Where Raymond of Tripoli rode after his charge through Saladin's ranks, says Ernoul.

places.name: Acre
places.note: Its bishop carried the True Cross at Hattin and was mortally wounded. Years later, says Ernoul, a Templar came to the lord of Acre and said he had buried the Cross; in 1191 two of Richard the Lionheart's officers came out from Acre to Saladin's camp, where the Cross was shown to them (Baha al-Din).

places.name: Jerusalem
places.note: The True Cross was brought from here to the army; the city surrendered to Saladin on 2 October 1187.

title: Cannae, 216 BC: The Gold Rings Hannibal Sent to Carthage
summary: The Battle of Cannae, 216 B.C., from the ancient writers who tell it: the heap of gold rings Hannibal's brother poured out at Carthage, in four sizes; Polybius and Livy, two witnesses who never saw the battle; eight legions and...

places.name: Cannae, the hill of Canne by the Ofanto (the ancient Aufidus)
places.note: The village of Cannae stood on a hill by the river Aufidus, today the Ofanto. The pin marks the hill, the traditional site; where the battlefield itself lay is debated (there are several versions, Mahaney 2024), and the river has moved about half a kilometre since.

places.name: Canusium (Canosa di Puglia)
places.note: About ten thousand survivors gathered here, Livy says; Busa fed and clothed them, and the young Publius Scipio made the nobles swear not to abandon the republic.

places.name: Carthage
places.note: Hannibal's brother Mago had the gold rings poured out in the entrance of the senate house here, Livy says; the senator Hanno asked him his questions.

places.name: Rome
places.note: The senate refused to ransom the prisoners Hannibal held, and thanked Varro because he had not despaired of the republic, Livy says.

title: Ain Jalut, 1260: Slave Soldiers Against the Mongols
summary: The Battle of Ain Jalut, 1260, from the sources on both sides: a captured Mongol general's last words, as a Persian history written for the Mongol court gives them; Hulegu's advance into Syria and his ultimatum to Cairo; why...

places.name: Ain Jalut (Ma'ayan Harod), at the foot of Mount Gilboa
places.note: The spring where the Mamluk army of Egypt met the Mongol force of Kitbuqa, on a Friday, the 25th of Ramadan, the 3rd of September 1260 in the Frankish chronicles. Where the lines stood is not known.

places.name: Aleppo
places.note: Stormed by Hulegu's armies in 1260; Bar Hebraeus compares the slaughter to that of Baghdad. Baybars passed through here as a captive boy.

places.name: Damascus
places.note: Opened its gates to the Mongols without a fight. Qutuz, too, had been sold here, by the Arabic accounts.

places.name: Cairo
places.note: Hulegu's envoys came here; al-Maqrizi says their heads hung on a gate of the city. Baybars was sold here to the Bunduqdar.

places.name: Acre
places.note: The crusader city the Egyptian army marched past; the Franks stayed out of the battle and agreed a price for Mongol horses.

places.name: Sidon
places.note: The Franks were furious with the Mongols over the damage they had done here, says a Frankish chronicle.

places.name: Sivas
places.note: Where the captured boy Baybars was taken after he was sold, on his way to Aleppo and Cairo.

places.name: Hama
places.note: In a much later story, a prince's mother here refused to buy the boy Baybars: there is evil in his eyes, she said.

places.name: Parwan, in what is now Afghanistan
places.note: The sultan Jalal al-Din beat a Mongol army here in 1221, as Juvaini, who wrote for the Mongols, records. Where exactly the battle was fought is not known; the pin marks the region.

places.name: Krak des Chevaliers
places.note: Taken by Baybars, eleven years after Ain Jalut.

title: The Lewis Chessmen: Why the Warders Bite Their Shields
summary: The Lewis chessmen, 93 pieces of walrus ivory and whale tooth found on the Isle of Lewis in 1831: 78 chessmen from at least four sets, 14 discs for another board game and a buckle; the find story that grew in the telling; Uig Bay...
tags: Lewis Chessmen National Museum of Scotland

places.name: Uig Bay, Isle of Lewis
places.note: Most accounts place the find on the sands of Uig Bay (the dunes at Ardroil). The exact find spot is not known.

places.name: Mealista, Isle of Lewis
places.note: On the same coast. Caldwell, Hall and Wilkinson (2009) see a strong possibility that the hoard was found here.

places.name: Trondheim
places.note: Seat of Norway's archbishop. Caldwell and colleagues name an important Scandinavian centre, especially Trondheim, as the likely place of making: a proposal, not a finding.

places.name: Skálholt
places.note: Seat of Bishop Páll in Iceland. Gudmundur Thorarinsson's Icelandic case points to his saga and Margrét the Adroit; he concedes it is circumstantial.

places.name: British Museum, London
places.note: Bought 82 pieces for 80 guineas after Madden knocked the price down from 100.

places.name: National Museum of Scotland, Edinburgh
places.note: The other eleven pieces arrived in 1888. The hoard was first shown at the Society of Antiquaries of Scotland in Edinburgh on 11 April 1831.

title: Krak des Chevaliers: The Best-Preserved Crusader Castle
summary: Krak des Chevaliers in Syria, the crusader castle that UNESCO's listing takes as the best preserved example of its period (its own summary says among the best preserved): the fortress of the Kurds of about 1030; the Hospitallers...

places.name: Krak des Chevaliers
places.note: Hisn al-Akrad, the fortress of the Kurds; held by the Hospitallers from the 1140s; besieged by Baybars from February 1271; the garrison marched out on 8 April 1271.

places.name: Homs
places.note: Around 1030 the emir of Homs put Kurdish soldiers in a fort on the hill. The castle guards the gap between the coast and Homs and Hama.

places.name: Hama
places.note: One of the two inland cities whose road to the coast the castle guarded (French Ministry of Culture).

places.name: Tripoli
places.note: Seat of the Count of Tripoli, who handed the castle to the Hospitallers in the 1140s; the letters of 1271 claimed to come from the Frankish leader there (Ibn al-Furat).

places.name: Aleppo
places.note: A corps of miners from Aleppo dug under the towers in the siege of 1271.

places.name: Acre
places.note: The Lord Edward, the future Edward I, landed here on 9 May 1271, one month after Krak fell (Deeds of the Cypriots).

places.name: Beaumaris Castle
places.note: One of the concentric castles Edward I built in Wales. Nothing we read puts Edward at Krak.

title: Knight's Armour: From Mail to Plate
summary: How knight's armour went from mail to plate, from the evidence: the mass graves of the Battle of Visby, 1361, where many of the dead were buried still wearing their armour, old mail hoods next to the latest plates; how mail was...

places.name: Visby, Gotland
places.note: On 27 July 1361 the army of the Danish king Valdemar Atterdag met the farmers of Gotland outside the town wall; four mass graves were found there between 1905 and 1930, nearly 1,200 people in three of them (Swedish History Museum). The exact positions of the graves are not shown.

places.name: Westley Waterless, Cambridgeshire
places.note: The brass of Sir John de Creke, who died around 1328; probably ordered by his son in the 1340s, so its armour is later than the man (Kinsey 2020).

places.name: Canterbury Cathedral
places.note: The gilded effigy of Edward, the Black Prince, who died in 1376; the helm, shield and gauntlets above the tomb are 1950s copies, the originals are in the crypt.

places.name: Milan
places.note: Where complete plate armour was probably first made, around 1400, the Met thinks.

places.name: Chalcis, Euboea
places.note: Pieces found in the ruins of the Venetian fortress here were put together in the 1920s into the Met's armour in the style of about 1400.

places.name: Glasgow
places.note: The Avant armour, the earliest near complete plate harness in the words of Ralph Moffat of Glasgow Museums; its helmet and right gauntlet are later, the left a twentieth century copy.

places.name: Royal Armouries, Leeds
places.note: Four fight interpreters from the Royal Armouries walked and ran on a treadmill in copies of armour from the mid to late 1400s (Askew, Formenti and Minetti, published 2011).

places.name: Agincourt
places.note: The treadmill study's authors say the cost of moving in armour may have contributed to the outcome there; Jaquet and colleagues point out the copies are later than the armour of Agincourt.

places.name: Prato
places.note: Home of the merchant Francesco Datini, who listed helmets and breastplates of proof and of half proof (Moffat 2024).

title: Mongol Invasion of Japan: What Sank Kublai Khan's Fleet?
summary: What sank Kublai Khan's fleet in the Mongol invasions of Japan, from the evidence: a famous scroll picture of a bomb bursting beside a samurai's horse, which the historian Thomas Conlan argues was painted in later, and the real...

places.name: Hakata Bay, Fukuoka
places.note: Where the fleet of 1274 landed and Takezaki Suenaga made his charge; in 1281 the wall along the bay kept the eastern army off the beach.

places.name: Takashima, Imari Bay
places.note: The southern fleet reached Imari Bay, by the island of Takashima, where the wind broke the ships. Three wrecks were confirmed on the seabed site off the island in 2011, 2015 and 2024; the exact positions are not shown.

places.name: Imazu, Fukuoka
places.note: One of the places where parts of the walls built from 1276 can still be seen today. Fukuoka City puts the total length along Hakata Bay at 20 kilometres.

places.name: Tsushima
places.note: Envoys were turned away here, and one party seized two Japanese men; in 1274 the fleet struck the island.

places.name: Iki
places.note: Struck by the fleet in 1274, on the way to Hakata Bay.

places.name: Kamakura
places.note: The seat of the shogunate, where Suenaga appealed to Adachi Yasumori and got his reward.

places.name: Kyoto
places.note: Where a courtier heard that a contrary wind had blown the fleet home; his own daily weather notes point to the winter monsoon, says Mizukoshi Mitsuharu.

places.name: Inner Shrine, Ise
places.note: A rumour said a wind god at Ise had sent the gusts; in 1293 the court raised his shrine in rank (Kawai 2021).

title: 172 Longbows from the Mary Rose: The Largest Collection Found
summary: The English longbows of the Mary Rose, sunk in the Solent on 19 July 1545: 172 yew bows, the only precisely dated English longbows we have; the arrows, spacers and bowstrings that came up with them; the first bow and the actor...

places.name: The Solent, off Portsmouth
places.note: The Mary Rose heeled over and sank here towards evening on 19 July 1545 (Van der Delft's letter, Letters and Papers XX i no. 1263). The marker is Portsmouth, not the wreck site: we have no coordinates for the wreck in our sources.

places.name: Southsea Castle
places.note: The Mary Rose Trust says Henry VIII watched the sinking from here. The castle has been much altered since 1545.

places.name: Abergavenny
places.note: Gerald of Wales says Welsh archers shot through an oak door of the castle almost a palm thick, and the arrows were left in the door in memory (Itinerarium Kambriae I.4).

places.name: Agincourt (Azincourt)
places.note: The battle of 1415, 130 years before the Mary Rose sank. How close its bows were to the Mary Rose bows, we do not know.

title: The Dardanelles Gun: The Giant Bombard That Unscrews in Two
summary: The Dardanelles Gun, a bronze bombard cast in 1464 for Sultan Mehmed II, in two halves of about seventeen tonnes that unscrew: the unscrewing on the beach at Chanak in 1868 (nearly 40 tons of force), the sixteen lever sockets...

places.name: Fort Nelson, Royal Armouries
places.note: Where the gun is today (Royal Armouries, Gallery 57). No year for its move here is given in our sources; the year marks its arrival in England.

places.name: Chanak (Çanakkale)
places.note: The open beach at Chanak where the crew of H.M.S. Terrible unscrewed the gun in January 1868 (log quoted by Lefroy); exact spot unknown.

places.name: Kilid Bahr (Kilitbahir)
places.note: The fort on the European shore; the gun stood in one or other of the forts at Chanak or Kilid Bahr (Royal Armouries). Year: Lefroy's list of the great guns at the straits, January 1868.

places.name: Constantinople (Istanbul), the land walls
places.note: Taken by Mehmed II in 1453; as far as we know, the great guns of the siege survive only in texts (Doukas, Kritovoulos, Leonard of Chios).

places.name: Adrianople (Edirne)
places.note: Where Doukas places the test shot of the great gun, in the winter before the siege.

places.name: Woolwich, the Rotunda
places.note: The Museum of Artillery, where Lefroy studied the gun in 1868.

places.name: Tower of London
places.note: Placed on the south side of the White Tower in 1930 (Royal Armouries, ffoulkes diary).

places.name: Ghent, Dulle Griet
places.note: The Flemish bombard Lefroy compared in 1868; year is his comparison, not the bombard's date.

title: The Bayeux Tapestry: What It Really Shows
summary: What the Bayeux Tapestry really shows, read scene by scene and checked against the written sources. It is an embroidery, not a tapestry: dyed wool on nine pieces of linen, 68.3 metres long by the Bayeux museum's measure. No maker...
tags: What Does the Bayeux Tapestry Show
Is the Bayeux Tapestry a Tapestry
How Long Is the Bayeux Tapestry

places.name: Bayeux
places.note: Odo's city, where the tapestry puts Harold's oath; its first sure record is an inventory of Bayeux Cathedral in 1476, and the museum in Bayeux keeps it.

places.name: Bosham
places.note: Earl Harold rides to Bosham and sails (captions HIC HAROLD MARE NAVIGAVIT).

places.name: Ponthieu
places.note: Count Guy's territory, where Harold landed and was seized. A region, not a town: the point only marks it near the Somme estuary.

places.name: Bonneville-sur-Touques
places.note: Where William of Poitiers puts Harold's oath, before the war in Brittany. The point is the modern village.

places.name: Rouen
places.note: Where Orderic Vitalis, a later writer, puts Harold's oath.

places.name: Pevensey
places.note: Duke William came to Pevensey (the caption); one version of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle says on the eve of Saint Michael's mass, 28 September 1066. The point is the modern village.

places.name: Hastings
places.note: The castle dug at Hastings (caption and Chronicle). The point is the modern town; the site of the battle of 14 October 1066 is not discussed in the video.

places.name: Canterbury
places.note: Most scholars think the hanging was made in England, probably in or around Canterbury, because its design draws on Canterbury manuscripts.

places.name: British Museum, London
places.note: As of November 2026, the hanging is on loan from France to the British Museum, until July 2027.

places.name: Reading Museum
places.note: Home of the full-size Victorian copy finished in 1886 by thirty-five women (a replica, not the original).

title: The Roman Shield
summary: What was the Roman scutum made of? Polybius describes a double layer of boards glued with bull-hide glue, linen, calfskin, iron edging and an iron boss; the shield from Tower 19 at Dura-Europos (before A.D. 256), which a 2011...
tags: What Was a Roman Shield Made of
How Heavy Was a Roman Shield

places.name: Dura-Europos, Syria
places.note: Town with a Roman garrison on the Euphrates, besieged and taken by the Persians, probably in 256; the painted scutum was found in Tower 19 in the 1932-33 season (Yale University Art Gallery 1933.715).

places.name: Dyrrachium (Durres, Albania)
places.note: Caesar against Pompey, 48 B.C.; the centurion Scaeva's shield with 120 holes (Caesar, Civil War 3.53). The fort's exact site is not known.

places.name: Nijmegen, Netherlands
places.note: A grave of about A.D. 90 to 95 with a shield boss, two rivets and an iron grip; the rivets give a board 4 to 5 mm thick (Koster 2010).

places.name: Harit (Kasr el-Harit), Fayum, Egypt
places.note: Find place of a whole shield published by Wolfgang Kimmig in 1940; never scientifically dated, maker unknown. Pin approximate.

places.name: Mouth of the Tyne, north-east England
places.note: A bronze shield boss of Junius Dubitatus, Eighth Legion Augusta, said to have been dredged up before 1877; the record dates it to Hadrian's reign (A.D. 117 to 138). Now in the British Museum.

places.name: Caerleon, Wales
places.note: Legionary fortress; a fragmentary goatskin shield cover, probably first or early second century (van Driel-Murray 1988).

places.name: Kalkriese, Germany
places.note: Early imperial shield remains scanned by a modern team (Schroeder, Petri and Zerbe 2022, as reported by S. Manning).

title: The Trebuchet: How It Really Worked
summary: How the trebuchet really worked, from the sources: the Warwolf at Stirling in 1304, where Edward I made a surrendered castle wait until it was struck; the two machines behind one name, a beam pulled by a crew on ropes and a beam...

places.name: Stirling Castle
places.note: Besieged by Edward I from April 1304; surrendered without conditions on 20 July 1304, and the king's order was that none of his people enter till it was struck with the Warwolf (Bain II no. 1560).

places.name: Perth
places.note: The king told his son to get lead for the siege from the churches around Perth and Dunblane, except over the altars (Bain II no. 1504).

places.name: Dunblane Cathedral
places.note: The churches around Dunblane were to give lead for the siege of Stirling (Bain II no. 1504); which churches is not recorded in our sources.

places.name: Toulouse
places.note: Simon de Montfort was killed besieging the city in 1218 by a stone from a machine pulled by women, says the Toulouse poem (Canso, lines 8448 to 8455).

places.name: Thessaloniki
places.note: The Avars' stone throwers, described by Bishop John in the Miracles of St Demetrius; the siege is dated 586 or 597, scholars disagree.

places.name: Krak des Chevaliers
places.note: Abu'l-Fida's 'fortress of the Kurds', where a great machine, a load for a hundred carts, was collected for the siege of Acre (standard identification).

places.name: Acre
places.note: The Mamluk army gathered siege machines for Acre in early 1291 (Abu'l-Fida).

places.name: Xiangyang
places.note: A counterweight machine built by an engineer from the west threw a stone of about 95 kilos; the Song commander surrendered the city (Yuan shi, juan 203).

places.name: Kenilworth Castle
places.note: Eight shots from the siege of 1266, 1 to 105 kg, found outside the walls; probably thrown by trebuchets (English Heritage).

places.name: Medieval Centre, Nykøbing Falster
places.note: Where a 12 tonne counterweight trebuchet was reconstructed in 1989; longest shot 168 m with a 15 kg ball (Hansen 1992).

title: How a Medieval Castle Was Built: "The Greatest Castle Never Built"
summary: How a medieval castle was built, told through one castle's paperwork: Beaumaris on Anglesey, begun for Edward I in 1295 and never finished. The letter of 27 February 1296 to the Exchequer (£500 short, workmen with nothing to live...
tags: How a Medieval Castle Was Built

places.name: Beaumaris Castle
places.note: Begun 1295 for Edward I beside the Menai Strait; never finished (Cadw).

places.name: Llanfaes
places.note: The Welsh port a mile from the castle, pulled down; the point is the modern village, the medieval town's extent is not known to us.

places.name: Newborough, Anglesey
places.note: The new town where many people of Llanfaes were forcibly resettled (Cadw); the year of the move is not given in our sources.

places.name: Conwy
places.note: Where the letter of 27 February 1296 was written (Morris 1901).

places.name: Caernarfon Castle
places.note: In June 1295 a hundred masons chosen at Chester were ordered here (Calendar of Close Rolls).

places.name: Harlech Castle
places.note: Putlog holes climbing in a spiral: Taylor's helicoidal scaffolding.

places.name: Chester
places.note: The justice of Chester was ordered to choose a hundred suitable masons.

places.name: Saint-Georges-d'Espéranche
places.note: Count Philip of Savoy's castle palace, very likely built under Master James; Edward was there in June 1273 (Saunders).

places.name: Yverdon
places.note: Taylor found Master James working here under his father, Master John, in the accounts of Savoy; before the Chillon payments, exact year not in our sources (Saunders).

places.name: Chillon
places.note: Payments to Master James here in 1266 to 1267 (Saunders).

places.name: Turin
places.note: The archives where Taylor searched the accounts of Savoy in 1950.

title: The Roman Pilum: Why the Javelin Bent
summary: Was the Roman pilum designed to bend? Caesar reports the iron bent in the Helvetii's shields in 58 B.C. but not why; Polybius gives the famous bending javelin to the light troops and says the pilum's iron would break before it...
tags: Was the Pilum Designed to Bend

places.name: Near Bibracte (Mont Beuvray)
places.note: Caesar fought the Helvetii near Bibracte (Gallic War 1.23 to 26); the exact site of the battle is uncertain, so the pin marks Bibracte.

places.name: Hod Hill, Dorset
places.note: Roman fort site where the British Museum's pilum head 1892,0901.1111 was found; the museum dates it to the middle of the first century A.D.

places.name: Grad near Šmihel, Slovenia
places.note: Hillfort with a hoard of at least 473 iron objects, mostly Roman weapons, dated to the end of the 3rd or the first half of the 2nd century B.C. Pin approximate.

places.name: Plain of Vercellae, northern Italy
places.note: Marius against the Cimbri, 101 B.C., where Plutarch places the change to the pilum; the exact site of the battle is uncertain, pin approximate.

places.name: Carthage
places.note: Polybius stood beside Scipio as Carthage burned in 146 B.C.

places.name: Bar Hill, Antonine Wall
places.note: Roman fort on the Antonine Wall; its excavators (report 1906) found 22 bent iron points, probably broken pilum heads, in its well. Year: the Wall's use in the mid 2nd century A.D.

title: The Roman Fort: 752 Men, No Beer, One Birthday

places.name: Vindolanda (Chesterholm), Northumberland
places.note: Roman forts from about A.D. 85; the writing tablets, first found in March 1973.

places.name: Coria (Corbridge)
places.note: 337 men of the First Cohort of Tungrians were at Coria on 18 May (Tab. Vindol. 154).

places.name: Housesteads
places.note: A playing-card fort on Hadrian's Wall, shown from the air.

places.name: Birdoswald
places.note: Building stone of A.D. 297 naming the praetorium and the principia (RIB 1912).

places.name: Hardknott
places.note: A fort that is more of a square than a playing card (English Heritage).

places.name: Newstead (Trimontium)
places.note: The fort dug by James Curle, who wrote in 1911 that fort plans show considerable variety.

places.name: Saalburg, Taunus, Germany
